To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
students with mild to moderate physical disabilities, but without intellectual disabilities, presented a positive self concept, self efficacy and realistic self evaluation.

(a) students with physical disabilities, irrespective of their level of cognitive functioning, exhibit a positive self concept profile; (b) students with physical, but not cognitive, challenges exhibit realistic self regulatory skills; (c) students with cognitive, but not physical, challenges exhibit unrealistic self regulation skills; and (d) students with combined physical and cognitive challenges exhibit unrealistic self regulatory skills, and a positive self concept.

students with mild physical disabilities, but without intellectual challenges, exhibited a realistic self concept and a positive self regulation profile, whereas students with considerable physical disabilities, but with normal intelligence, presented a negative self concept, but realistic self regulation, and students with mild to moderate cognitive challenges, in combination with considerable physical disabilities exhibited unrealistic self regulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the self regulation profile of students with physical and cognitive disabilities.

the development of self regulation in children and adolescents with physical disabilities and the relationship of motor and mental (dis)abilities with the development of specific aspects of self regulation.
the self concept and self regulatory aspects (e.g., goal setting, self-efficacy, self-evaluation) of students with physical disability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

students with physical disabilities, irrespective of their intellectual functioning, can be expected to present self regulation profiles which differ from the profiles presented by their non disabled peers, but also from each other.
the self concept and self regulatory profiles of students with physical (dis)abilities are highly dependent on their motor and cognitive abilities.
the relationship between self regulation and motor and cognitive abilities is not a simple one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the students with mild to moderate intellectual and motor disabilities, who have a positive, yet unrealistic self concept, may benefit the most from a self regulation intervention.
the students with mild motor disabilities and without cognitive challenges had a positive and realistic self concept and a positive self regulation profile.
the self concept of students with physical and intellectual disabilities is a function of the severity of their physical and cognitive challenges.
The main takeaway from our work is that
students with motor disabilities should be encouraged to set realistic, but challenging, goals, and to evaluate their performance in relation to these goals.
students with physical disabilities, especially those who also present with intellectual disabilities, are capable of developing self regulatory skills and a positive self concept.
students with physical disabilities, especially those with mild to moderate motor disabilities, should receive instruction on self regulation.
